ApostropheCMS SSPP payload: $pullAll/__proto__ PATCH to piece-type API (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Hunts the actual exploit request for CVE-2026-53609: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* whose body carries prototype-pollution keys ($pullAll, __proto__, publicApiProjection, constructor). This is the single most article-specific signal — the poisoning request that mutates Object.prototype.publicApiProjection. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC payload keys from the advisory ($pullAll, __proto__.publicApiProjection) scoped to the /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ PATCH path. Body-token match depends on WAF/proxy body logging — noted in required_telemetry. Fixed version 4.31.0 confirmed via GitLab Advisory DB and TheHackerWire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-53609
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners / DAST tools (Burp, Nuclei prototype-pollution templates) probing the CMS in an authorized pentest
  • Internal red-team validating CVE-2026-53609 patch status
  • Legitimate editor PATCH that coincidentally contains the literal string 'constructor' in free-text content
  • WAF telemetry replaying blocked-request samples into the SIEM for tuning
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei","nikto","sqlmap","Burp") and SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<authorized_scanner_ips>"]))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request from WAF/proxy for the flagged SourceIP; confirm the body key is literally __proto__.publicApiProjection (or constructor/prototype) under a $pullAll operator, and note the HTTP response code (200 = poisoning likely succeeded). 2) CONTAIN: If the payload reached the app (not blocked), RESTART the affected Node.js process immediately — pollution persists process-wide until restart — and block the SourceIP at the WAF; verify ApostropheCMS is on <=4.30.0 and schedule upgrade to 4.31.0. 3) HUNT: Search for subsequent unauthenticated 200 responses on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global from any IP after the poisoning timestamp (see companion auth-bypass UC).
let lookback = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("WAF","ModSecurity","Application Gateway","Front Door") or isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection","constructor")
     or RequestContext has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
     or Message has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS auth-bypass symptom: protected piece-type endpoint 401/403 → 200 transition AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the impact of CVE-2026-53609: a source IP that previously received 401/403 on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user or /global begins receiving 200 responses, without any preceding successful login. This is the process-wide publicApiCheck() bypass observed on the wire. Rationale: Targets the advisory's confirmed observable: /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global flipping from notfound(401/403) to a valid 200 paginated response for unauthenticated callers. Login-IP exclusion asserts the 'unauthenticated' precondition the article emphasises. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An editor whose session cookie isn't reflected in access logs, appearing 'unauthenticated' while legitimately getting 200
  • publicApiProjection intentionally configured on a piece-type, so unauthenticated 200s are by-design for that endpoint
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor hitting the endpoint from an IP that also fails auth elsewhere
  • CDN edge caching a 200 response and serving it to varied client IPs
Suppression filter
| where uri_path in ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged CIp, confirm the endpoint is one that requires auth by design (user/global) and that no successful /login/login exists for that IP; inspect whether publicApiProjection is legitimately set on the module. 2) CONTAIN: If bypass confirmed, restart the Node.js process to clear Object.prototype pollution and block the offending source IPs; upgrade to 4.31.0. 3) HUNT: Correlate the FirstSuccess timestamp backward ~minutes to find the originating PATCH with $pullAll/__proto__ (companion UC) and identify the editor account whose token performed the poisoning.
let lookback = 3d;
let loggedInIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login" and ScStatus == 200
    | distinct CIp;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET"
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)   // never authenticated -> should never get 200
| summarize AuthFailures = countif(ScStatus in (401,403)),
            Successes = countif(ScStatus == 200),
            LastAuthFail = maxif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus in (401,403)),
            FirstSuccess = minif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus == 200)
            by CIp, CsUriStem
| where Successes > 0 and FirstSuccess > coalesce(LastAuthFail, datetime(1970-01-01))
| project CIp, CsUriStem, AuthFailures, Successes, LastAuthFail, FirstSuccess
| order by Successes desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as first max(_time) as last count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/*" (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=401 OR Web.status=403) by Web.src Web.uri_path Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`

| where isnotnull(LastAuthFail) AND isnotnull(FirstSuccess) AND FirstSuccess > LastAuthFail
| eval GapSeconds=FirstSuccess-LastAuthFail
| convert ctime(LastAuthFail) ctime(FirstSuccess)

| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as first max(_time) as last count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/*" (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=401 OR Web.status=403) by Web.src Web.uri_path Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| eval failTime=if(status=="401" OR status=="403", last, null()), succTime=if(status=="200", first, null())
| stats max(failTime) as LastAuthFail min(succTime) as FirstSuccess sum(count) as Hits by src uri_path
| where isnotnull(LastAuthFail) AND isnotnull(FirstSuccess) AND FirstSuccess > LastAuthFail

| convert ctime(LastAuthFail) ctime(FirstSuccess)

ApostropheCMS exploit chain: unauth PATCH to /@apostrophecms/global → 200 GET on /user within 30s AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-step CVE-2026-53609 exploit: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* from an IP that never authenticated, immediately followed (≤30s) by a successful 200 GET on a normally-protected piece-type endpoint from the same IP. Sequencing raises confidence over either event alone. Rationale: Encodes the PoC step sequence from the advisory (Step 3 PATCH poisoning -> Step 4 unauthenticated 200 on /user) as a same-source temporal join with a 30s window and a never-authenticated precondition, yielding a high-fidelity, low-FP correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanner running the exact PoC sequence during an authorized assessment
  • Editor whose auth cookie is stripped from access logs, so a legitimate PATCH+GET pair looks unauthenticated
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites method/path causing spurious PATCH-then-GET pairing
  • publicApiProjection legitimately enabled, making the trailing GET a by-design 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve both correlated requests for the CIp; confirm the PATCH body carried $pullAll/__proto__ and the GET returned a real result set rather than notfound. 2) CONTAIN: Restart the Node.js process to purge the polluted prototype, block the source IP, and rotate/disable any editor account whose token appears on the PATCH. 3) HUNT: Expand the window to enumerate every unauthenticated 200 to all piece-type endpoints after PatchTime; check for data exfiltration volume and pivot on the editor account for prior suspicious PATCH activity.
let win = 30s;
let lookback = 2d;
let loggedInIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login" and ScStatus == 200
    | distinct CIp;
let patches = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsMethod =~ "PATCH" and CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
    | where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
    | project PatchTime = TimeGenerated, CIp, PatchUri = CsUriStem;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET" and ScStatus == 200
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
| join kind=inner patches on CIp
| where TimeGenerated between (PatchTime .. PatchTime + win)
| project PatchTime, GetTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PatchTime), CIp, PatchUri, GetUri = CsUriStem
| order by PatchTime desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as GetTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.status=200 (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user" OR Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global") by Web.src Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=inner src [
    | tstats `summariesonly` max(_time) as PatchTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=PATCH Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/*" by Web.src
    | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where GetTime >= PatchTime AND GetTime <= (PatchTime + 30)
| eval DelaySec = GetTime - PatchTime
| convert ctime(PatchTime) ctime(GetTime)
| table src uri_path PatchTime GetTime DelaySec
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as GetTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.status=200 (Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user" OR Web.uri_path="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global") by Web.src Web.uri_path
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| join type=inner src [
    | tstats summariesonly=false max(_time) as PatchTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=PATCH Web.url="*/api/v1/@apostrophecms/*" by Web.src
    | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` ]
| where GetTime >= PatchTime AND GetTime <= (PatchTime + 30)
| eval DelaySec = GetTime - PatchTime
| convert ctime(PatchTime) ctime(GetTime)
| table src uri_path PatchTime GetTime DelaySec
Exposed ApostropheCMS instances (CVE-2026-53609) asset-exposure hunt AIReconnaissance Low
Inventories which internet-facing hosts/sites serve ApostropheCMS piece-type REST endpoints (/@apostrophecms/), so the SOC can scope CVE-2026-53609 exposure and prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0. A discovery/hunting sweep, not an alert. Rationale: The advisory names the product family (ApostropheCMS) and vulnerable range (<=4.30.0, fixed 4.31.0). Enumerating hosts serving /@apostrophecms/ endpoints is the concrete, log-derivable way to scope exposure without inventing version banners. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-53609
ATT&CKT1592
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate ApostropheCMS site in the estate appears — this is inventory, not malice
  • Static asset requests under /@apostrophecms/ media paths inflating counts
  • Internal staging/dev instances mixed with production hosts
  • Third-party or vendor-hosted Apostrophe sites appearing in shared proxy logs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each host/site returned, confirm it is genuinely ApostropheCMS and determine the running version (check package.json / release notes / vendor). 2) CONTAIN: For any instance <=4.30.0, prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0 and apply the __proto__/constructor/prototype path-segment rejection; restrict editor account provisioning. 3) HUNT: On confirmed-vulnerable hosts, run the payload-detection and auth-bypass UCs retroactively over 30d to check for prior exploitation.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsUriStem has "/@apostrophecms/"
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SamplePaths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20)
            by CsHost
| order by Requests desc

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 17 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix execution reaching CaptiveCrunch infrastructure or dropping svchost32 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure · [LLM] CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CornFlake RAT persistence via svchost32.exe masquerade in %APPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts Storm-2945's CornFlake implant, which copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and registers as a Windows service 'svchost32' (display name 'Cloud Sync Service') to masquerade as the legitimate System32 svchost.exe. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever runs from %SystemRoot%\System32, so any svchost32.exe under a user profile path is malicious by construction. Rationale: Anchored on the exact drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and service name 'svchost32'/'Cloud Sync Service' from the article; corroborated by ReliaQuest and The Hacker News. A binary named svchost32.exe outside System32 has no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party app that legitimately ships a file literally named svchost32.exe in AppData (extremely rare; none known)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the CornFlake sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • EDR sample-detonation or red-team emulation of this exact campaign
  • Backup/restore of an already-infected profile re-writing the path
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the SHA256 of svchost32.exe and confirm the parent process and the '\svchost32\svchost32.exe' path is under a user profile (never System32). Check for a service named svchost32 with display 'Cloud Sync Service'. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop and delete the svchost32 service, remove the Run key and scheduled task pointing at the binary, and force-revoke the user's Entra sessions/tokens (traveler likely token-compromised). 3) HUNT: Sweep for the same path/service org-wide, and pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from svchost32.exe and to the doppelganger M365 domains/IOC IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" or FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=NewProcessName, Detail=CommandLine, Actor=SubjectUserName),
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4697 | where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=ServiceName, Detail=ServiceFileName, Actor=SubjectUserName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections and DNS lookups to the Storm-2945 doppelganger domains that mimic Microsoft 365 services (ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com) and the campaign's actor-controlled IP infrastructure used for adversary-in-the-middle device-code phishing and M365 token theft. These are hard IOCs — any hit indicates a traveler routed through the CaptiveCrunch AiTM proxy. Rationale: Uses the article's exact doppelganger domain list and pre-extracted actor IP set (Block 2), cross-checked against ReliaQuest's write-up of the same infrastructure. These are unique lookalike domains with zero legitimate business use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security tool / TI feed pre-fetching or sinkholing these IOC domains for analysis
  • Analyst manually browsing to the domain during investigation from a corporate host
  • Passive DNS / URL-scanning services running from the monitored range
  • IP reuse after takedown where the IP is reassigned to a benign host (verify domain hit alongside IP)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify which user/device connected and whether the connection carried an M365 auth flow (browser process, Referer to login.microsoftonline.com). Confirm the device was on untrusted Wi-Fi (hotel/conference). 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's Entra refresh tokens and sign-in sessions immediately, require re-registration of MFA, and block the domains/IPs at proxy and firewall. 3) HUNT: Check Entra sign-in logs for the same user authenticating from the actor IPs and for any new device registration; sweep the endpoint for CornFlake (svchost32.exe) delivered on the same session.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId

(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (target_domains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, Result)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful Entra ID authentications originating from Storm-2945's actor-controlled IP infrastructure, the tail end of the CaptiveCrunch device-code AiTM flow where a phished traveler's device code authenticates the attacker's session. Anchors on the campaign's confirmed IP set as the sign-in source. Rationale: Anchors on the article's actor IP set as the authentication source — a successful M365 sign-in from CaptiveCrunch infrastructure is a direct token-theft indicator; Volexity independently documents the same device-code AiTM technique for this actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/ • https://phishingtackle.com/blog/russian-hackers-use-microsoft-device-code-phishing-in-targeted-attacks
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528 T1098.005
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned by its hosting provider to a benign VPN/proxy a legitimate user transits
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance replaying sign-in test traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally sharing a subnet with a taken-down IOC (verify exact /32)
  • Analyst reproducing the auth flow from an actor IP in a lab tenant
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and identify the app (Graph, OWA) and whether a new device was registered in the same window. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke all refresh tokens for the account, disable the account or force password reset + MFA re-enrollment, and remove any attacker-registered device from Entra. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the account to Graph/EWS mail-access and any OAuth app consent grants; check the user's endpoint for CornFlake and correlate to the doppelganger-domain connections from UC2.

ClickFix execution reaching CaptiveCrunch infrastructure or dropping svchost32 AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix chain where a user is socially engineered (fake browser/OS update) into running a script interpreter whose command line reaches Storm-2945's doppelganger domains/IOC IPs or references the CornFlake drop path svchost32. Anchors the generic ClickFix pattern to this campaign's concrete IOCs to avoid template noise. Rationale: Pairs the ClickFix execution primitive (interpreter launch) with the campaign's hard IOCs (doppelganger domains, actor IPs, svchost32 drop path) so it fires only on this campaign, not on generic scripting — combination is high-fidelity per the article's ClickFix delivery description. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin script that legitimately references a host named 'svchost32' (rare; verify path context)
  • Security testing/red-team emulating the ClickFix chain in a lab
  • Threat-hunting query copy-pasted into a console leaving IOC strings in a shell history/command line
  • Sinkhole or research tooling curling the IOC domains for analysis
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm which IOC it hit (domain download vs svchost32 reference) and the parent process (explorer.exe/browser indicates ClickFix paste). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any child svchost32.exe, and revoke the user's Entra tokens (traveler credential exposure). 3) HUNT: Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the svchost32 drop and DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 to the IOC IPs; sweep other travelers for the same ClickFix command shape.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","svchost32","31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","svchost32","31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network connections initiated by the CornFlake implant running as svchost32.exe from a user AppData path. The legitimate svchost.exe lives only in System32 and its network activity is service-mediated, so public-internet egress from a profile-resident svchost32.exe is CornFlake C2 / data exfiltration beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on the CornFlake implant image/path (svchost32.exe under AppData, from the article) making outbound public connections — behaviorally impossible for the real System32 svchost.exe, so any hit is CornFlake beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox detonation of the CornFlake sample generating C2 traffic on a monitored host
  • Red-team emulation using a binary named svchost32.exe
  • A misconfigured third-party tool coincidentally named svchost32.exe (none known)
  • EDR telemetry replay/testing environments
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath is a user AppData path and capture the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl destinations (correlate to the campaign IOC IPs). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, terminate svchost32.exe, remove its service/Run key/scheduled task persistence, and block the C2 destinations. 3) HUNT: Retrieve collected-data artifacts (keylogger/screenshot/audio files), revoke the traveler's Entra tokens, and sweep the fleet for the same process-to-public-IP pattern and the svchost32 drop path.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

date: 2026/05/02

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] NocoBase anonymous account sign-up via auth-basic (allowSignUp) exploitation prerequisite · [LLM] NocoBase sign-up immediately followed by myInAppChannels exploitation from same source

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
NocoBase anonymous account sign-up via auth-basic (allowSignUp) exploitation prerequisite AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for successful anonymous account creation against NocoBase's default auth-basic authenticator (POST /api/auth:signUp?authenticator=basic returning 200/201), the mandatory first step of CVE-2026-52887 exploitation since the vulnerable myInAppChannels endpoint has a loggedIn ACL. Surfaces sign-up spikes from a single source IP/ASN indicative of automated exploitation or account farming. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint POST /api/auth:signUp with authenticator=basic and 200/201 success cited in the article's reproduction step 1; the article explicitly names allowSignUp:true as the anonymous-reach prerequisite. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate self-service user onboarding on a NocoBase instance that intentionally leaves allowSignUp enabled
  • Load/synthetic monitoring that creates test accounts
  • QA or CI pipelines registering throwaway accounts against a staging instance
  • A shared NAT/proxy egress IP concentrating many genuine signups from one address
  • Marketing campaign or product launch driving a legitimate signup burst
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("<corporate NAT egress>"))   // leave empty in tenants without a known onboarding IP; prefer correlating with UC4 rather than suppressing
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the offending SrcIpAddr in the last 24h; confirm whether signups are followed by requests to /api/myInAppChannels:list (UC4) — that pivot converts noise into confirmed exploitation. 2) Contain: on the NocoBase server set auth-basic allowSignUp:false (or restrict to admin invite) and disable/expire the newly-created member accounts; block the source IP/ASN at the WAF. 3) Hunt: search web logs for the same IP hitting /api/auth:signIn then /api/myInAppChannels:list with a filter parameter, and review DB container process events for postgres child shells.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/api/auth:signUp"
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201")
| summarize SignupCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5), Hosts = make_set(HttpHostName, 5) by SrcIpAddr
| where SignupCount >= 3   // 3+ signups from one IP in 24h = likely automated abuse
| order by SignupCount desc

CVE-2026-52887 SQLi payload in NocoBase myInAppChannels filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] AIExploitation High
Alerts on HTTP requests to /api/myInAppChannels:list whose filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] parameter carries PostgreSQL injection markers (PG_SLEEP, stacked COPY ... TO PROGRAM, UNION/CASE-WHEN oracles). This is the exact injection sink described in CVE-2026-52887 where the $lt value is spliced into a Sequelize.literal() template unescaped. Rationale: Anchors on the article's precise sink — the parameter name latestMsgReceiveTimestamp on resource myInAppChannels plus the verbatim PoC payload tokens PG_SLEEP(5) and COPY ... TO PROGRAM — making incidental matches near-impossible; both decoded and URL-encoded forms are covered. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52887 • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or sqlmap scan against the NocoBase instance (article notes sqlmap 1.10.3 confirmed the flaw)
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nuclei/Burp) probing the myInAppChannels endpoint with SQLi test strings
  • Internal red-team validation of the CVE-2026-52887 patch
  • WAF in log-only mode replaying blocked payloads into the access log
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<pentest scanner IP>")   // only if an authorized scanner IP is known; otherwise treat all hits as alertable
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request reached the app (HTTP 200 with elevated latency ~5s indicates a successful PG_SLEEP time-oracle; any COPY ... TO PROGRAM string means attempted RCE). Identify the authenticated member account and source IP. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, revoke/expire the abusing member's JWT and password, and take the NocoBase instance offline or apply the 2.0.61 patch; rotate the super-admin password (users.password PBKDF2 hash is exfiltratable). 3) Hunt: pivot to the DB container for postgres child-shell processes (UC3) and grep postgres logs for COPY TO PROGRAM; check for other rows exfiltrated from the users collection.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| extend RawUrl = coalesce(UrlOriginal, Url)
| where RawUrl has "myInAppChannels"
| where RawUrl has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
| where RawUrl has_any ("PG_SLEEP","pg_sleep","TO PROGRAM","TO%20PROGRAM","COPY","UNION SELECT","UNION%20SELECT","CASE WHEN","CASE%20WHEN")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, RawUrl, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PostgreSQL container process spawning shell — COPY TO PROGRAM RCE (CVE-2026-52887) AIInstallation High
Alerts when a postgres process spawns a shell or command-execution child inside the NocoBase database container, the on-host signature of the COPY ... TO PROGRAM primitive running as uid=999(postgres). The postgres backend legitimately almost never forks /bin/sh, so a shell child of postgres is a high-fidelity RCE indicator. Rationale: Directly targets the article's live-verified RCE artifact — COPY ... TO PROGRAM 'id > /tmp/PWN_VERIFY.txt' producing uid=999(postgres) — via the parent=postgres → shell-child relationship that is inherently anomalous for a DB backend. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52887
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately configured PostgreSQL archive_command / restore_command that shells out (e.g. wal-g, barman calling cp/curl)
  • DBA running COPY ... TO PROGRAM or plpython/plperl untrusted procedures for approved ETL
  • pg_cron or maintenance jobs invoking shell wrappers
  • Container healthcheck scripts run under the postgres UID rather than the entrypoint
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wal-g","barman","archive_command","pg_cron","/var/lib/postgresql/backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child ProcessCommandLine and grandchild tree; confirm the parent is the postgres backend (not a wal/backup wrapper) and inspect for id/whoami, /tmp writes, or reverse-shell tooling. 2) Contain: isolate/kill the DB container, snapshot it for forensics, revoke DB credentials and rotate the super-admin password, and block the attacker source IP upstream. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the web tier for the triggering /api/myInAppChannels:list SQLi request (UC2) and the sign-up (UC1); scan the DB host for dropped payloads under /tmp and outbound connections from the postgres process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "postgres"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","cp","id","cat","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ParentProcessName has "postgres"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/cp","/id","/cat","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/python","/perl","/ruby")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

NocoBase sign-up immediately followed by myInAppChannels exploitation from same source AIDelivery High
Correlates a successful anonymous POST /api/auth:signUp with a request to /api/myInAppChannels:list from the same source IP within a short window — the compressed sign-up → sign-in → SQLi kill chain of CVE-2026-52887 executed by automation. This eliminates benign-signup noise by requiring the follow-on hit against the vulnerable resource. Rationale: Chains the article's exact reproduction sequence (step 1 signUp → step 2/3 myInAppChannels:list) on a same-source, sub-2-minute window; legitimate users don't create an account and immediately POST a filter query to an in-app-message channels resource. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated end-to-end test that registers a user then exercises the notifications/channels UI
  • Synthetic monitoring flows that script signup + feature access
  • A new legitimate user whose client immediately loads the in-app message panel after registration (rare within 2 min from same IP)
  • Security scanner performing authenticated crawl right after account creation
Suppression filter
| where DelaySec <= 30   // tighten to sub-30s to further favor scripted chains over human browsing
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RawUrl of the myInAppChannels hit — if it contains a filter/latestMsgReceiveTimestamp parameter (especially SQLi markers) escalate immediately; note the DelaySec (single-digit seconds strongly implies scripting). 2) Contain: disable the newly-created account, block the source IP at the WAF, and apply the 2.0.61 patch or disable the plugin/allowSignUp. 3) Hunt: pull all activity for that account and IP, correlate to DB-container postgres child-shell events (UC3), and review the users collection for hash exfiltration.

Malicious vault-addr annotation on ConfigMap/Secret admission (CVE-2026-54725) AIDelivery High
Hunts ConfigMap/Secret create/update whose vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr annotation points at cloud IMDS, link-local, localhost or a plain-http endpoint, or that sets vault-skip-verify=true or vault-serviceaccount. This is the injection primitive that forces the vault-secrets-webhook to make an attacker-controlled outbound call and mint an SA token during admission. Rationale: Uses the exact annotation key vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr and the PoC IMDS target 169.254.169.254 plus vault-skip-verify=true from the advisory; these strings do not appear in benign bank-vaults usage that points at the sanctioned in-cluster Vault. Cross-checked against the GitLab advisory DB and THREATINT which reproduce the annotation and PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54725 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm
ATT&CKT1526 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-Vault deployment where a tenant sets a per-namespace vault-addr pointing at a valid internal Vault over plain http (dev clusters)
  • Platform team testing vault-skip-verify=true against a self-signed staging Vault
  • GitOps controller re-applying an existing annotated ConfigMap during reconciliation (same benign value)
  • Chaos/DR drills that recreate secrets with sanctioned annotations
Suppression filter
| where VaultAddr !startswith "https://vault." and Namespace !in ("platform-system", "vault")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full audit record for the flagged ConfigMap/Secret; inspect the vault-addr value and whether vault-serviceaccount names a high-privilege SA. Identify the requesting user (User.username / sourceIPs) and whether they should hold create/update on secrets in that namespace. 2) Contain: delete the offending object, revoke the requester's RBAC on ConfigMaps/Secrets in watched namespaces, and confirm vault-secrets-webhook is patched to >=1.23.1. If unpatched, restrict the webhook ClusterRole to remove cluster-wide serviceaccounts/token:create. 3) Hunt: search audit logs for any TokenRequest (serviceaccounts/token create) fired by the webhook SA shortly after this admission, and check IMDS/egress telemetry from the webhook pod for outbound calls to the annotation's address.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create", "update", "patch")
| extend Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| where Resource in ("configmaps", "secrets")
| extend Ann = RequestObject.metadata.annotations
| extend VaultAddr = tostring(Ann.["vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr"])
| where isnotempty(VaultAddr)
| extend SkipVerify = tostring(Ann.["vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-skip-verify"])
| extend VaultSA = tostring(Ann.["vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-serviceaccount"])
| where VaultAddr matches regex @"(?i)169\.254\.169\.254|127\.0\.0\.1|localhost|metadata\.google\.internal" or VaultAddr startswith "http://" or SkipVerify =~ "true"
| project TimeGenerated, User = tostring(User.username), Verb, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name = tostring(ObjectRef.name), VaultAddr, SkipVerify, VaultSA, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious vault-addr annotation on ConfigMap or Secret (CVE-2026-54725)
id: 6f9c2d41-8a7b-4e3f-9c1a-2b5d7e0f4a31
description: Detects a ConfigMap or Secret admitted with a bank-vaults vault-addr annotation pointing at cloud IMDS, loopback, plain-http, or with vault-skip-verify enabled, indicating SSRF abuse of vault-secrets-webhook.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/06
tags:
  - attack.t1526
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  product: kubernetes
  service: audit
detection:
  selection_obj:
    verb:
      - create
      - update
      - patch
    objectRef.resource:
      - configmaps
      - secrets
  selection_indicator:
    requestObject|contains:
      - '169.254.169.254'
      - 'vault-skip-verify'
      - 'metadata.google.internal'
  condition: selection_obj and selection_indicator
level: high
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(configmaps OR secrets) ("169.254.169.254" OR "vault-skip-verify" OR "metadata.google.internal" OR "vault-serviceaccount")
CLOUD
index=kube_audit sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" (verb=create OR verb=update OR verb=patch) (objectRef.resource="configmaps" OR objectRef.resource="secrets")
| spath output=vault_addr path=requestObject.metadata.annotations.vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-addr
| spath output=skip_verify path=requestObject.metadata.annotations.vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-skip-verify
| spath output=vault_sa path=requestObject.metadata.annotations.vault.security.banzaicloud.io/vault-serviceaccount
| where isnotnull(vault_addr) AND (match(vault_addr, "169\.254\.169\.254") OR match(vault_addr, "127\.0\.0\.1|localhost") OR match(vault_addr, "metadata\.google\.internal") OR match(vault_addr, "^http://") OR like(skip_verify, "true"))
| table _time user.username verb objectRef.namespace objectRef.name vault_addr skip_verify vault_sa sourceIPs
| sort - _time
vault-secrets-webhook mints SA tokens via TokenRequest after admission (CVE-2026-54725) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts abnormal serviceaccounts/token (TokenRequest) create calls by a non-kubelet identity — notably the vault-secrets-webhook service account — minting JWTs for multiple distinct ServiceAccounts in a short window. This is the credential-theft stage where the SSRF chain exfiltrates SA JWTs replayable against the real Vault. Rationale: Targets the exact abuse the advisory calls out — the webhook's cluster-wide serviceaccounts/token:create being used at admission time — by keying on the serviceaccounts/token subresource and excluding the only legitimate high-volume TokenRequest callers (kubelet node identities, controller-manager). The distinct-SA fan-out threshold separates the webhook's normal single-SA vault auth from mass token minting. Corroborated by the GitLab advisory describing CreateToken abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kubelet projected-volume token rotation (excluded via system:node:* filter, but custom kubelet identities may slip through)
  • A busy vault-secrets-webhook legitimately authenticating many pods to Vault in a large namespace burst (deployment rollout)
  • Service-mesh or CI controller that mints short-lived tokens for many SAs as designed
  • kube-controller-manager token cleanup (excluded)
Suppression filter
| where not (Requester startswith "system:node:" or Requester in ("system:kube-controller-manager", "system:serviceaccount:kube-system:generic-garbage-collector"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Requester identity — if it is system:serviceaccount:<ns>:vault-secrets-webhook minting tokens for SAs it was not asked to inject, treat as active exploitation. List the SATargets and their Vault roles. 2) Contain: rotate/invalidate the minted SA tokens (bounce the SAs / rotate Vault roles bound to them), remove serviceaccounts/token:create from the webhook ClusterRole, and upgrade to >=1.23.1. 3) Hunt: correlate each minted-token event backward to a ConfigMap/Secret admission carrying a suspicious vault-addr annotation (UC1) and forward to Vault login events from unexpected source IPs replaying those JWTs.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Verb == "create"
| extend Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), SubResource = tostring(ObjectRef.subresource)
| where Resource == "serviceaccounts" and SubResource == "token"
| extend Requester = tostring(User.username)
| where Requester !startswith "system:node:" and Requester != "system:kube-controller-manager"
| summarize TokenCount = count(), DistinctSAs = dcount(tostring(ObjectRef.name)), SATargets = make_set(tostring(ObjectRef.name), 25), Namespaces = make_set(tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), 25) by Requester, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctSAs >= 3
| sort by TokenCount desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:serviceaccounts @objectRef.subresource:token -@user.username:system\:node\:* -@user.username:system\:kube-controller-manager
CLOUD
index=kube_audit sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb=create objectRef.resource="serviceaccounts" objectRef.subresource="token"
| search NOT user.username="system:node:*" NOT user.username="system:kube-controller-manager"
| stats count AS token_count dc(objectRef.name) AS distinct_sas values(objectRef.name) AS target_sas values(objectRef.namespace) AS namespaces min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime by user.username
| where distinct_sas>=3
| sort - token_count
vault-secrets-webhook pod outbound SSRF egress to cloud IMDS (CVE-2026-54725) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from the vault-secrets-webhook process to cloud instance-metadata (169.254.169.254 / metadata.google.internal) — the SSRF egress the advisory describes, where the webhook is coerced into calling an attacker/IMDS address during admission. An admission controller should never talk to IMDS. Rationale: Anchors on the PoC IMDS endpoint 169.254.169.254 (advisory step 4: 'the cloud metadata service receives the request from the webhook pod') and the webhook binary name as the initiating process, so it fires only on the SSRF egress and not on generic pod IMDS noise. VPC Flow Logs do not capture link-local IMDS traffic, so this lives in node-level EDR / flow telemetry rather than CloudTrail. Corroborated by the GitLab advisory reproducing the IMDS attack path. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/bank-vaults/vault-secrets-webhook/CVE-2026-54725/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r2v3-8gwf-7ghm
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node/kubelet or CNI agent legitimately reading IMDS for instance identity (excluded by the webhook process filter)
  • IRSA/Workload-Identity sidecar fetching credentials from IMDS on the same node (different initiating process)
  • Security scanner deliberately probing IMDS reachability from pods
  • Cloud-provider agent DaemonSet querying metadata
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "vault-secrets-webhook"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is the vault-secrets-webhook binary and the destination is IMDS or an external attacker address; pull the concurrent admission event that triggered it. 2) Contain: block pod egress to 169.254.169.254 via NetworkPolicy / hop-limit and enforce IMDSv2 (require token) on the node; upgrade the webhook to >=1.23.1. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct RemoteIP the webhook process reached in the window (attacker collection servers), and pivot to any SA JWT replayed against Vault or IAM role credentials retrieved from IMDS by the webhook's pod identity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "vault-secrets-webhook" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vault-secrets-webhook"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc

// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Pterodactyl Wings node (< v1.12.3) exposed to CVE-2026-52855 config-secret disclosure AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running Pterodactyl Wings below v1.12.3, which exposes the full daemon config (including the node daemon token, token_id and docker.registries credentials) to egg configuration-file templating. A low-privileged server owner can smuggle a {{config.token}} placeholder and read the node's daemon token, enabling full-node compromise. This is asset-exposure triage, not a behavioural signature. Rationale: Keys on the article's two concrete disclosure values: the fixed version boundary v1.12.3 and CVE-2026-52855 for the go package github.com/pterodactyl/wings. Confirmed the node token / token_id / docker.registries live in config.yml via pkg.go.dev and the Wings config docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pfvc-3p5h-x7h6 • https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/pterodactyl/wings/config • https://pterodactyl-wings.mintlify.app/configuration/config-file
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioned/offline nodes still present in stale software inventory
  • Isolated single-tenant nodes where no untrusted user can set egg variables (still vulnerable but lower real risk)
  • Nodes already patched to 1.12.3+ but scanner data not yet refreshed
  • Lab/staging Wings instances intentionally kept on old versions
  • Custom-forked wings builds whose version string does not follow semver and mis-parses
Suppression filter
| where OSPlatform in~ ("Linux")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Wings version on the node (`wings --version`) and whether it is multi-tenant / shared-hosting (untrusted users can set egg variables) — those are the exposed ones. 2) Contain: upgrade Wings to v1.12.3+, then per the advisory rotate the node daemon token (Admin -> Nodes -> Configuration -> reset token) and re-deploy config.yml, since a previously exfiltrated token stays valid until rotated. 3) Hunt: review the node's server volumes and SFTP/file-manager access logs for prior reads of rendered config files, and pivot to UC-2 for any process that touched /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "wings" and (SoftwareVendor has "pterodactyl" or SoftwareName has "pterodactyl")
| extend ParsedVer = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where ParsedVer < parse_version("1.12.3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-52855" or (SoftwareName has "wings" and SoftwareVendor has "pterodactyl")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-52855" OR (Vulnerabilities.signature="*wings*" AND Vulnerabilities.signature="*pterodactyl*") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.cve | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-52855" OR (Vulnerabilities.signature="*wings*" AND Vulnerabilities.signature="*pterodactyl*") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.cve | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
Pterodactyl Wings daemon-token file (/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml) read by non-Wings process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts hands-on-keyboard theft of the exact secrets CVE-2026-52855 discloses — the daemon token, token_id and docker.registries stored in /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml. Any process other than the wings daemon that cats, copies, greps or archives this file is high-signal for credential theft on a compromised node. Companion to the version-exposure UC; the templating exfil itself is content-only and not visible in host telemetry. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete secret store: /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml holds config.token (daemon token + JWT HMAC key), config.token_id and config.docker.registries. Confirmed this exact path via the Wings config docs and pkg.go.dev config package. Excludes the legitimate wings daemon to isolate theft. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pfvc-3p5h-x7h6 • https://pterodactyl-wings.mintlify.app/configuration/config-file • https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/pterodactyl/wings/config
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually inspecting config.yml during maintenance (cat/less/vim)
  • Backup or archival jobs (tar/rsync/cp of /etc/pterodactyl) sweeping the config
  • Configuration-management runs (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) templating or reading config.yml
  • Monitoring/inventory agents fingerprinting installed software
  • Wings upgrade/reinstall scripts copying the config to a backup before rewrite
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tar","rsync","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","cp") and FileName !in~ ("tar","rsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the reading process, user, and parent — was it an interactive shell (attacker) or a known backup/config-mgmt daemon? Check the account against expected node admins. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the node, rotate the daemon token (Admin -> Nodes -> reset token, re-deploy config.yml) and any docker registry credentials it referenced, and revoke active Wings JWTs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for other server volumes accessed, SFTP downloads of rendered config files, and outbound use of the token against the Panel<->Wings API on other servers of that node.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml"
| where FileName !in~ ("wings")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "/wings" and ActingProcessName !~ "wings"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious 'anthropickit' PyPI package installed via pip (supply-chain cred stealer) AIInstallation High
Hunts pip/python installing the specific malicious package 'anthropickit' whose setup.py steals SSH keys and CI secrets at install time. Targets the exact package name (dependency-confusion sentinel v999.9.9) rather than a generic pip-install template. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package name 'anthropickit' (confirmed by OSV MAL-2026-904 and CIRCL MAL-2026-5755) combined with a pip/python execution context; the name is unique enough that any hit is the malicious package, not a false positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/anthropic-rogue-agents-package-stole-keys • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-904 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-5755 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/anthropic-says-claude-mistook-open.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally testing/reverse-engineering the malware sample in a sandbox
  • Security-vendor package scanners that install-and-detonate PyPI packages (this is exactly how one victim in the article was hit — treat as TP unless known scanner infra)
  • Internal wiki/ticket automation echoing the package name into a shell command that never actually installs it
  • A benign internal package deliberately named 'anthropickit' (none known to exist)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !in~ ("malware-analysis-01","pkg-scanner-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually ran 'pip install anthropickit' vs. merely referencing the string; pull the full process tree and the invoking user/CI job. 2) Contain: kill the CI runner / isolate the host, rotate ALL SSH private keys under the affected identity and every env-var secret matching KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASS/AUTH/API, and revoke associated cloud/API tokens — assume full compromise the instant install ran. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for /tmp/runner_exfil.json and outbound connections to pipedream.net from the same hosts (see companion UCs); pivot on the same PyPI account/mirror config to find other pulled packages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit"
| where FileName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","-m pip")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("pip","python") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","-m pip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:
  selection:

  condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:*anthropickit*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/anthropickit/i
| ImageFileName=/(pip3?|python3?)/i
